citations.citation: "Eliza Emily Chappell, the First Chicago Teacher Paid by Public Funds in 1833." Digital Research Library of Illinois History Journal, 19 January 2018.
what_it_does_not_supply: NO SITE THAT AGREES WITH ITSELF, and this is why the identification stays inferred. The page's own opening line says "The Eliza Chappell School was roughly at Lake and Clark Streets are today" — which is where the school MOVED in 1834, not the log house it started in.

No way past the three-way conflict it sits in: Andreas puts a log school-house west of State Street between South Water and Lake (data/structures/chappel_infant_school.json), drloih_beaubien puts the first room in Beaubien's cabin at Lake and Market, and this page carries the third reading.
No footnote, no dimension, and no description of the room itself.
what_it_supplies: THE SCHOOL'S FIRST ROOM AND THE DATE IT LEFT IT: "Chappell arrived in Chicago in June 1833 with the prospects of opening a school by September. The school was established in a small log house formerly used as a store... In 1834, the school was moved into the First Presbyterian Church in Fort Dearborn, on the southwest corner of Lake and Clark Streets."
A LOG HOUSE FORMERLY USED AS A STORE is the phrase that joins to drloih_beaubien's cabin, let first to Philo Carpenter for a drug store and then, in 1833, to Chappel's school.

The school as it was kept: 25 students who furnished their own chairs, no desks, some paddling canoes across the river to it, and "maps, a globe, scriptural texts and hymn books, and illustrations of geometry and astronomy" for teaching tools.
The marriage: Chappel married the Rev. Jeremiah Porter on 15 June 1835, sixteen days before the scene date.

THE CHAPPEL SHORE DRAWING'S IMMEDIATE SOURCE (T-0909): the post's first image is the uncredited drawing deposited as eliza_chappel_school_shore_view, same filename, captioned "The Eliza Chappell School was roughly at Lake and Clark Streets are today." It republishes the drawing and supplies none of its artist, date or original publication.

citations.citation: John Moses and Joseph Kirkland (eds.), History of Chicago, Illinois, vol. 2 (Chicago and New York: Munsell & Co., 1895). Read here for the town before 1836: the Chicago Democrat's second office in Chapter I, 'The Press'; the school section sale and Granville T. Sproat's school in the education chapter at printed page 103 and before it; Cook county's first term of court, Richard J. Hamilton's house and the Caton & Collins partnership in 'The Bench and Bar' at pages 150-157; the first and second drug stores in the medical chapter; the first Sunday school, the first Baptist and Episcopal organizations, Tippecanoe Hall and Father Walker's cabin in the church chapters at pages 294, 348-349, 367 and 374-375; the Miller brothers' tannery, Blodgett's brick yard and the Jones & King hardware firm in the manufactures chapters at pages 406-407, 441 and 450-456; and Dr. Temple's building and stage line in the memoirs after page 624.
what_it_does_not_supply: MOST OF WHAT IT WAS FETCHED FOR, AND MORE DECISIVELY THAN VOLUME 1. Of the forty-nine lead surnames the Newberry index flagged against this WORK, nine earned a claim here, nineteen appear only outside the pre-1836 window, and the remaining twenty-one are in the window for a reason that is not the early town - a forename, an adjective, a noun, a table of contents, or a man born after the scene date. The full row-by-row result, with each row's volume 1 verdict beside its volume 2 one, is at data/research/books/moses_kirkland_v2_lead_surnames.json.

A CHICAGOAN NAMED GUNN, WHICH IS THE ONE NEGATIVE THIS READING WAS FOR. Volume 1 recorded `gunn` ABSENT and said on itself that the absence was from one book of two. Volume 2 prints it fourteen times and every one is Dr. Moses Gunn, born 1822. The surname is in the work; the Chicagoan is not.

AN INDEPENDENT VOICE. It is the second volume of the compilation whose first volume this project already reads, by the same editors in the same year, and it cites Andreas by name on the pages read here. Where a sentence credits another work the claim says so and the citation belongs to that work.

A STREET ADDRESS IN THE MODERN SENSE. Positions here are corners, a side of a branch, a distance from a river bank, a block between two cross streets, and a relation to a tavern, a house or a fort - and the street NAMES are the names of 1895, which the compiler flags himself with 'what is now'.

A DATE FOR TIPPECANOE HALL, which is the one placed building here that cannot be carried into the scene. The southeast corner of Kinzie and State streets is stated; when the building was fitted up for worship is 'Later', after 19 October 1834, and nothing narrows it.

CONSISTENCY WITH ITS OWN FIRST VOLUME. Volume 1 makes Benjamin Hall the proprietor of the town's first tannery, arriving 1830; volume 2 makes the Miller brothers its builders in 1831 and Hall a partner in 1832. Volume 1 has John Dean Caton renting the back room and attic of the Temple building and sub-letting desk-room to Giles Spring; volume 2 has him with a desk in the office and a sleeping room in the attic. Both readings of each are recorded and neither is adopted.

ANYTHING ABOUT THE POTAWATOMI THAT THIS PROJECT MAY USE. The chapters read here are the press, the courts, medicine, education, the churches and the trades, and where they touch 1835 at all they touch the settlers' institutions. The standing constraint in AGENTS.md is unchanged by this reading and nothing here was taken as licence to depict anyone.
what_it_supplies: TWO DATED PRESENCE LISTS, which is what this project is thinnest in. The catalogue of the fourteen Baptists present at the organization of the First Baptist society on 19 October 1833, with the denominator beside it (twenty-five Baptists in the settlement), at printed page 294. And the eleven gentlemen who organized the first Episcopal congregation in 1834, eight of whom formed its vestry, at page 348.

AN INDUSTRIAL SITE THE PROJECT DOES NOT HOLD, placed: Tyler K. Blodgett's brick yard, the first in the city, established in the spring of 1833 on the north side, not far from the river bank, between Dearborn and Clark streets, with Henry S. Lampman as its workman.

A TANNERY PLACED BY A BUILDING THE PROJECT HOLDS, and a disagreement with volume 1 about who built it: John and Samuel Miller built it in 1831 JUST NORTH OF SAMUEL MILLER'S TAVERN near the junction of the two branches, and Benjamin Hall became a PARTNER in 1832 - where volume 1, quoting Blanchard, has Hall as the proprietor of the first tannery, arriving 1830.

A RESIDENCE WITH A BLOCK: Richard J. Hamilton built his house on what the compiler of 1895 calls Michigan street between Cass and Rush, at about 1833, and lived in it for nineteen years; before that he lived in the fort and then in the Agency House.

A SECOND ADDRESS FOR THE CHICAGO DEMOCRAT'S OFFICE - a room over the hardware store of Jones & King, a few doors from its first location, about the end of its first year of publication - and the firm dated independently to 1834, which is what makes the relation usable.

TWO BUILDINGS USED AS SCHOOLS AND ONE AS A COURTROOM: the First Baptist church, a small frame building on South Water street near Franklin, occupied on weekdays by Granville T. Sproat's English and classical school for boys; the old stable near the Agency House, where John Watkins was hired in 1833 to teach the little school; and an unfinished loft in the Mansion House, directly north of the Tremont House of 1895, where Cook county's first term of court sat in 1834.

A BUILDING WITH A BUILDER, A NEIGHBOUR AND A CONDITION, which is rare: the small frame building Mark Beaubien erected near Mr. Noble's house, which on 19 August 1832 had neither doors nor windows and was very imperfectly roofed, and which held the town's first Sunday school.
A FIGURE FOR THE LAND THE TOWN WAS BUILT ON: the Chicago school section sold in October 1833 for $38,895, on the petition of three-fourths of the township's legal voters.
A SECOND DRUG STORE, which volume 1 does not mention at all: Dr. Edmund Stoughton's, established in the spring of 1833, after Philo Carpenter's of late 1832.
A CONSTRUCTION YEAR FOR A BUILDING THE PROJECT HOLDS: Dr. Temple put up the Temple building in 1833, and ran a Chicago-to-Peoria stage line out of its office from 1834, with a timetable.

endings.text: The north-bank school written down, and the District No. 4 meeting copied out for 7 July. Two answers to one household question: a school already teaching, and one still to be argued over. The note is the story's.

No school written down yet, but the notice is copied out: 7 July, six in the evening, the Presbyterian Church. Whether a school house is built is for the meeting to say. The note and the waiting are the story's.

The north-bank school is written down, but the river lies between it and the stores, and that is a long way each morning for a child of five. The question stays open for the youngest. The note is the story's.

The north-bank school is written down: a walk and a river crossing each morning, no great thing for a child of ten. Whether there is room for one more scholar is a question for another day. The note is the story's.
Nothing written down and nothing copied: the question goes home as it came. The schools you passed are history, the meeting is next week, and the asking is the story's.

evidence.locator: Vol. 1, the schools chapter, the Eliza Chappel paragraph (archive.org scan p. 431, as read in docs/research/04-structures-south.md § 9).
evidence.text: Andreas has Eliza Chappel's infant school of 1833–34 in a log house just outside the military reservation, divided into school-room and lodging quarters.

evidence.locator: Digital Research Library of Illinois History Journal, 19 January 2018, the paragraph beginning 'Chappell arrived in Chicago in June 1833' (accessed 2026-09-04).
evidence.text: An unfootnoted 2018 online history says Chappell opened her school in a small log house formerly used as a store, and that in 1834 it moved into the First Presbyterian Church at Lake and Clark.

evidence.reasoning: Andreas gives only 'just outside the military reservation', whose western line on the south side was State Street until February 1835. The structure record chooses a point inside that two-block strip and grades it reconstructed; the online history and the Beaubien-cabin reading disagree on the site, so the stop says other accounts differ and claims no front door.
evidence.text: The log house is placed on the west side of State Street between South Water and Lake; the lot is not documented, and other accounts put the school's first room at Lake and Market or at Lake and Clark.

evidence.reasoning: The structure record's phase carries the house to 1835 as an inference about how long a sound log house lasts, and its occupants field ends Chappel's use in 1834. The stop therefore narrates the school as history and says nothing of who is inside.
evidence.text: On 1 July 1835 the log house is inferred to stand; the school had left it in 1834 and no source names anyone in it in 1835.

evidence.locator: Vol. 1, archive.org scan p. 305 (as read in docs/research/04-structures-south.md § 9 and docs/research/03-structures-north.md).
evidence.text: Andreas has John Watkins employed by Colonels Hamilton and Owen in 1833 to teach near the old Indian agency-house, and later in a house on Michigan Street between Cass and Rush.

Moses and Kirkland say Richard J. Hamilton, with Colonel Owen, hired John Watkins in 1833, and about then built his house on what is now Michigan Street between Cass and Rush, where he lived for nineteen years.

evidence.reasoning: The same employers, teacher, year and block face appear in both histories; neither names the other's house, and Moses and Kirkland give no side of the street. The structure record makes the identification as an inference, sets the house mid-face and grades the coordinate reconstructed, and its function says the school use is unattested by 1835.
evidence.text: The house Watkins taught in and the house Hamilton built are read as one house on the north side of Michigan Street; its lot is not documented and no class in it in 1835 is recorded.

evidence.locator: Vol. 1, the schools chapter, the paragraph citing Mr. Wells's report (as quoted in data/structures/north_side_school_1833.json and docs/RESEARCH/north_side_school_1833.md § 1).
evidence.text: Andreas reports from Mr. Wells's report that Hamilton and Owen built a house on the north bank of the river, just east of Clark Street, in which Watkins continued his school, the first house built for a school in Chicago, but adds that this does not recur to Watkins's recollection.

evidence.locator: Vol. 1, the schools chapter, the 1835 paragraph following George Davis's school in the Presbyterian church (archive.org scan p. 433, as read in docs/research/04-structures-south.md § 9).
evidence.text: Andreas says that in 1835 John Watkins was teaching what had become a public school on the North Side, on the river bank just east of Clark Street, in the building Hamilton and Owen erected in 1833, and that the exact date of his retirement is not known.

evidence.reasoning: The schools chapter's 'just east of Clark Street' is adopted because it is the more specific statement, made twice, in the chapter about the building; the structure record keeps the other reading as a stated uncertainty, so the stop speaks of the bank and the year, not a door or a July class.
evidence.text: The school-house is placed on the North Water Street frontage just east of Clark; Andreas's Methodist chapter puts 'the Watkins school-house' between Clark and LaSalle, about a block west.

evidence.locator: 26 Nov 1833 (Vol. I No. 1), the imprint; Andreas vol. 1, the press chapter on Calhoun's office.
evidence.text: The Democrat's first issue, 26 November 1833, gives its office as the building on the corner of South Water and Clark streets; John Calhoun printed it there.

evidence.locator: 20 May 1835 (Vol. II No. 5), p. 4, col. 6, the colophon (transcription lines 4177–4180). Transcription-mediated reading.
evidence.text: By 20 May 1835 the Democrat's colophon gives the office as over Messrs. Jones & King's hardware store, in South Water Street, so the corner is a former office on the scene date.

evidence.locator: 1 July 1835, p. 3, col. 5 (extracted claim chicago_democrat_1835_07_01#c012); first printed 17 June 1835, p. 3, col. 3 (chicago_democrat_1835_06_17#c006). Transcription-mediated reading of a damaged column.
evidence.text: The Democrat of 1 July 1835 prints a notice, dated 17 June: a meeting of the inhabitants of School District No. 4 will be held on Tuesday 7 July at 6 o'clock P.M. in the Presbyterian Church, to consider measures for building a school house in the district and to elect a trustee.

The household, its question about a child of five or ten, the route, what is written down or copied, the endings, the timing inputs and the A Schooling Note keepsake are invented connective narrative. No pupil, teacher, fee or answer is documented, and no named person is met.

opening.text: Your household has one question: where could a child learn? Ride past the places Chicago's first classes met, ending where the Democrat was printed. The household is invented; the schools are documented.

premise: Ride past the places Chicago's first classes met, on both sides of the river, with an invented household's question about school, and finish with a notice in the Democrat dated today.
